expected cost of a refusal, $h(\theta)g(x)$, falls with truthfulness,
so the incremental cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)$ falls with
$\theta$.  The familiar certification sorting is therefore the
opposite of the statement in the text: a higher $\theta$ makes the
strict auditor relatively cheaper, $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ in the
weak sense.

In particular there is no interior $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$; the strict monotone
decreasing relation $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty on $(0,1)$.  In the
weak ordering the lenient auditor is optimal on the whole non-truthful
range $\theta\in[0,1)$, and on the discrete support $\{0,1\}$ this is
the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$ for the malpractice type with the
knife-edge indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the truthful type.  Up to
the conventional tie-breaking the common belief that a reputable audit
certifies truthfulness is reversed in the $x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)$
specification: truthfulness makes the strict auditor relatively
cheaper, the only payoff relevant non-generic point being the
indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at $\theta=1$.  This is the usual
$\theta$-independent ranking $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, strictly
preferred for every $\theta<1$ and indeterminate at $\theta=1$, i.e.
formally the strict comparative static is empty and the weak
dominance is the whole interior $\theta<1$, in the binary model the
strictly interesting type $\theta=0$. ∎

14.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the x-independent tax the expected outlay is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x),$$

with $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and
$g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$.  For the binary technology

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(1)\ge0,$$

and with $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0.$$

Hence
$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$
and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ is therefore strictly
cheaper than the strict auditor $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the
two auditors are payoff equivalent only at the truthful pole $\theta=1$
where the refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ is shut down.

In particular
$$\frac{d}{d\theta}\big[(1-\theta)F(\theta)\big]=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,$$
so $\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  The (expected) cost
of moving from the lenient to the strict auditor falls with truthfulness,
i.e. the advantage of staying with the lenient auditor is strongest for
the most untruthful types and is dissipated as $\theta\to1$.  On the
conventional support this is the whole interior

$$x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad 0\le\theta<1,$$

with indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top type.  In the discrete
support $\{0,1\}$ this is the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$ and the weak
preference $x^{*}(1)\in\{0,1\}$; with the usual tie-breaking in favour of
the cheaper auditor the lenient auditor is the weakly dominant choice for
the whole admissible range and the strict preference for leniency is
confined to the imperfectly truthful part of the support, $\theta<1$,
i.e. $\theta=0$ on the two point model.  That is the familiar “bad types
buy the soft auditor’’ region, the only non-generic point being the
degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.  The textbook $xp(x)$ increasing
story is not guaranteed here because $p$ is stated decreasing in $x$,
so the sign of $g'(x)$ and hence the usual monotone comparative static
on $x^{*}(\theta)$ cannot be taken for granted without further restriction
on $p$.  Up to the conventional weak ordering the lenient auditor is the
optimal choice for every $\theta<1$.

2.text:
With the $x$ independent tax written out the expected outlay of a type
$\theta$ which hires $x$ is

$$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+\Pr\{{\rm no\;report}\}\,p(x)F(\theta)
          =t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) , \qquad x\in\{0,1\}, $$

so that up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$

$$ \widetilde C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta )g(x),\qquad 
 h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;g(x)=xp(x)\ge 0 .$$

$1-\theta$ and $F$ are decreasing so that $h(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing on $[0,1]$, $h(1)=0$, and $h(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.
On the two point technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

hence

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
       =h(\theta )g(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,$$

and with $p(1)>0$, $F>0$

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff \theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0.$$

In particular

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\quad\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1), $$

i.e. $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the
two auditors are payoff equivalent at the truthful pole.  Up to the
$x$ free term the $x$ ranking is the ranking of $g(x)=xp(x)$ and is
$\theta$ independent,

$$\arg\min_{x}C(\theta ,x)=\arg\min_{x}g(x),$$

so that on the admissible support

$$x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad0\le\theta<1,
 $$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is undetermined.  In the monotone sense

$$\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]\le0,$$

$h'(\theta)<0$, so that $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $-C$
has increasing differences.  Hence

$$ \theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}),$$

the (weak) comparative static is $x^{*}\uparrow$ in $\theta$.  The
expected cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ is
strictly decreasing in $\theta$ on $[0,1)$,

$$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
\;\;\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},$$

so the aversion to a strict auditor is strongest for the most
untruthful types and vanishes at $\theta=1$.  In the strict
preference sense

$$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;\Rightarrow\;x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$$

never occurs on the interior of the support.  On the discrete
support $\{0,1\}$ the strict preference for the lenient auditor is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$, $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$, and the truthful type
$\theta=1$ is indifferent, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  Weakly the lenient auditor
$x=0$ is optimal for the whole non-truthful part $0\le\theta<1$, i.e.
in the usual statement $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with the degenerate
indifference at $\theta=1$.  This is the opposite of the conventional
"more truthful firms buy a lenient auditor" story; the model gives the
reverse, essentially flat, sorting $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ in $\theta$,
the strict monotone decrease being empty.  Up to the conventional weak
ordering this is quoted as the lenient auditor being (weakly) dominant
on $[0,1)$, strictly dominant on $0\le\theta<1$ and indeterminate at the
truthful limit $\theta=1$. ∎

12.text:
The $x$–free tax can be dropped for the auditor choice.  With
${\rm Pr}\{{\rm no\;report}\mid\theta ,x\}=x(1-\theta)$

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+{\rm Pr}\{{\rm no\;report}\}p(x)F(\theta)
          =t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) ,
\end{equation*}
and up to $t(\theta)$

\begin{equation*}
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;\;g(x)=xp(x)\ge0 .
\end{equation*}

$F$ decreasing and $1-\theta$ decreasing imply $h$ strictly decreasing
on $[0,1]$ with $h(1)=0$ and

\begin{equation*}
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,
\end{equation*}
in the monotone sense.  Hence on the $x$–part the firm minimises
$g(x)$.  On the admissible binary support

\begin{equation*}
g(0)=0,\qquad g(1)=p(1)>0,
\end{equation*}
so that $g$ is strictly increasing in the discrete sense and

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=h(\theta)g(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
\end{equation*}
$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$.  In particular

\[
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
\]
and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The incremental cost of moving from the
lenient to the strict auditor is

\[
\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)>0,\qquad\theta<1,
\]

and $\Delta(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ because
$(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing.  Hence the expected
penalty cost of strictness falls with truthfulness,

\[
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =\bigl[-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)\bigr]
   \bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0,
\]

i.e. $C$ is sub-modular and $-C$ has increasing differences in
$(\theta,x)$.  The usual monotone comparative static is therefore

\[
x^{*}(\theta)\le x^{*}(\theta'),\qquad\theta<\theta',
\]

the more truthful type is weakly more willing to bear the refusal
risk of the strict auditor.  On the two point support

\[
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
\]

and $x^{*}(1)$ is undetermined, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  In strict
monotone terms

\[
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing,
\]

the optimal auditor is flat at the lenient choice on the whole
interior.  Up to the degenerate indifference at the top, $h(1)=0$, the
weak preference for leniency is the unique minimiser on the
non-truthful part of the support, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  In the
binary $\{0,1\}$ formulation this is the strictly preferred lenient
choice $x^{*}(0)=0$ and the indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the
perfectly truthful pole $\theta=1$.  The conventional ‘more truthful
$\to$ more lenient’ sorting is therefore reversed; the aversion to
the strict auditor is strongest for the most untruthful types and
vanishes only at $\theta=1$.  This is the usual flat, i.e.
$\theta$-independent, ranking $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, the only
payoff-relevant non-strict point being the indifference $\Delta(1)=0$.
∎

4.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the expected outlay of a $\theta$-firm is

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+{\mathbb P}\{{\rm no\;report}\}\,
{\mathbb P}\{{\rm RS\;audit}\mid{\rm no\;report}\}F(\theta )
     =t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) ,
\end{equation*}
so that with

\begin{equation*}
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0 ,\qquad k(x)=x\,p(x)\ge 0,
\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)k(x) ,
\qquad h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0 ,
\end{equation*}
on $[0,1]$ and $h(1)=0$.  The $x$-choice is the choice of $k(x)$ and
$t(\theta)$ is $x$-irrelevant.  On the admissible binary technology

\begin{equation*}
k(0)=0,\qquad k(1)=p(1)>0,
\end{equation*}
and

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)
      =h(\theta)k(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,
\end{equation*}
with

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0 .
\end{equation*}
In particular

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  Hence with the usual tie breaking

\begin{equation*}
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}
and $x^{*}(1)$ is undetermined, $C(1,0)=C( 1,1)$.  The incremental
cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in truthfulness,

\begin{equation*}
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\big[h(\theta_{2})-h(\theta_{1})\big]<0,\qquad
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
\end{equation*}
so that

\begin{equation*}
C(\theta',x')-C(\theta',x)-C(\theta,x')+C(\theta,x)
   =\big[h(\theta')-h(\theta)\big]\big[k(x')-k(x)\big]<0,
\qquad\theta'>\theta,\;x'>x,
\end{equation*}
i.e. $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$.  In the usual $-C$ order
$x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$.  In the strict
preference sense there is therefore no interior $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$
with $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ on $\{0,1\}$; the optimal
policy is flat at the lenient auditor on the whole non-truthful part of
the support.  Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ is the strictly optimal
choice for every non-truthful type $\theta<1$, the only degenerate point
being the truthful pole $\theta=1$ where the refusal channel is shut
down and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  On the binary support $\{0,1\}$ this is the
strictly distinct malpractising type $\theta=0$ with weak continuation
to the whole interval $[0,1)$, i.e. the conventional statement that the
expected cost of a refusal $(1-\theta)F(\theta)p(1)$ is decreasing in
truthfulness so that the aversion to strictness is strongest for the
most untruthful types and the more truthful type is weakly more willing
to bear the stricter audit.  The strict monotone decrease
$\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Rightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ is
empty; up to the trivial indifference at $\theta=1$ the familiar
“strict auditor is relatively cheaper for the good type’’ sorting
$x^{*}(\theta)\!\uparrow$ is obtained.  This is the familiar
reverse-certification result, the only non-generic point being the
indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the fully truthful limit. ∎

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$, and $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for every

$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$,

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The strict cost advantage of the lenient auditor

$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$

and $h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$, so the

 =h(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$,

so up to t(θ) the firm minimises

E(θ,x)= (1-θ)F(θ) × x p(x) = w(θ) g(x) ,

Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=w(θ)p(1)=(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)≥0

C(θ,0)<C(θ,1)  ⇔  (1-θ)p(1)F(θ)>0  ⇔  θ<1,

statement.  With the normalisation x=0 lenient, x=1 strict,

x*(θ)=0  for every 0≤θ<1,

with the conventional indifference at the top type θ=1, C(1,0)=C(1,1).

malpractising type θ=0,

C(1,0)-C(0,0)=p(1)F(0)>0 ,      C(1,1)-C(0,1)=0,

so the strict preference for leniency is attained at θ=0 and is
weakly maintained on the whole non–truthful part of the support.

interior region θ∈[0,1), i.e. θ<1, on which the expected penalty loss
from a refusal, w(θ)g(x), is positive and strictly decreasing in
θ.  The weight w(θ)=(1-θ)F(θ) is strictly decreasing, so a marginal
increase in truthfulness reduces the (expected) cost of the refusal
event and makes the lenient choice relatively more attractive on the

Up to the $x$ free term $t(\theta)$ the expected bill of a $\theta$-type is

$$
C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta )+ {\rm Pr}\{ {\rm no\;report}\}\,
{\rm Pr}\{ {\rm RS\;audit}\mid {\rm no\;report}\}\,F(\theta)
          =t(\theta )+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta) ,   \qquad x\in\{0,1\},
$$

i.e. up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x)\ge0 .
$$

$1-\theta\downarrow$ and $F\downarrow$ so that in the monotone sense

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

and $h(\theta)\downarrow0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$.  Hence the $x$–choice is
independent of $t(\theta)$ and

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=h(\theta)g(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
      =\Delta(\theta)\ge0 ,
$$

with $\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ under the normalisation
$p(1)>0,F(\theta)>0$.  In particular

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+\Delta(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$; the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the
strict auditor $x=1$ for every non truthful type and the two auditors
are payoff equivalent at the top type.  Up to the irrelevant $t(\theta)$

$$
\ell(\theta,x)=h(\theta)g(x),\qquad 
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
   =h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0,
$$

on the usual interior where $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $g'(x)>0$.  $C$ is
submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and $-C$ is supermodular, so that in the
minimisation order

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\;\Longrightarrow\;x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge
x^{*}(\theta_{1}),
$$

the optimal strictness is weakly increasing in truthfulness.  On the
binary support

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=0\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is undetermined, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The incremental cost
of strictness

$$
\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ in the monotone sense,
$\Delta(\theta_{2})<\Delta(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$,
so the aversion to strictness is weakest for the most truthful firms
and vanishes at $\theta=1$.

In particular there is no interior strict single crossing
$x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$.
In the strict preference sense the monotone comparative static
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty on $[0,1]$.  Weakly the lenient auditor is
the unique cost minimiser on the whole non-truthful interior,
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with the degenerate indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the truthful pole.  On the discrete support
$\{0,1\}$ this is the familiar statement that the (strict) preference
for $x=0$ is the malpractice type $\theta=0$, with weak domination
$x=0$ for every $\theta<1$ and indifference at $\theta=1$.  This is the
reversal of the common belief: the more truthful the accounts the
smaller the weight $h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ attached to the
no-report risk and hence the (weakly) weaker aversion to a strict
auditor. ∎

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta )
       =h(\theta )g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta ):=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;

$$

$$

and, with the normalisation $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$,

h(\theta)g(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

with

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

and

  =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0
  \qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ in the monotone sense.
Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

i.e. the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the strict auditor
$x=1$ for every non truthful type and the two auditors are payoff
equivalent at the truthful pole $\theta=1$ where the refusal risk
$x(1-\theta)$ is shut down.  Up to the degenerate indifference at
$\theta=1$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

so that on the admissible support the $x$–choice is flat in $\theta$.
In monotone comparative statics

$$
\frac{\partial^{2}C}{\partial\theta\partial x}
 =h'(\theta)g'(x)<0\iff g'(x)>0,
$$

so $C$ is submodular, $-C$ is supermodular and the usual Topkis
ordering gives $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$.  The
expected cost of a refusal, $h(\theta)g(x)$, falls with truthfulness,
so the incremental cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)$ falls with

opposite of the statement in the text: a higher $\theta$ makes the
strict auditor relatively cheaper, $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ in the

\[

   \bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0,

\[
x^{*}(\theta)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,

Up to the $x$ free tax the expected outlay of a $\theta$-firm is

on $[0,1]$ and $h(1)=0$.  The $x$-choice is the choice of $k(x)$ and

\begin{equation*}

and

      =h(\theta)k(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0 ,

\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}

x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
\end{equation*}

C(θ,0)=t(θ), C(θ,1)=t(θ)+(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)
Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)=h(θ)p(1)≥0,
Δ(θ)=0⇔θ=1, Δ(θ)>0 for θ<1.

Hence on the admissible support 
C(θ,0)<C(θ,1) ∀θ<1, C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
x*(θ)=0 for 0≤θ<1 and x*(1) is indifferent. The x-ranking is the 
ranking of g(x). With the two points g(0)=0<g(1)=p(1)>0, argminₓC(θ,x)=
argminₓg(x) is θ-independent. 

h(θ) is strictly decreasing, so Δ(θ) is strictly decreasing in θ on 
[0,1) and Δ(θ)→0 as θ↑1. The expected refusal loss (1-θ)F(θ)p(1) falls 
with truthfulness, so the aversion to strictness is strongest for the 
most untruthful types. In the usual Topkis form ∂²C/∂θ∂x=
h′(θ)[p(x)+xp′(x)]≤0 when g′>0. The model as written gives the 
submodular ordering C submodular in (θ,x) and -C with increasing 
differences, i.e. x*(θ) is weakly increasing in θ. In particular 
θ₂>θ₁ ⇒ x*(θ₂)≥x*(θ₁). 

Strict monotone decrease x*(θ₂)<x*(θ₁) for θ₂>θ₁ never occurs on the 
admissible support. On the discrete support {0,1} the strictly 
interesting case is θ=0: C(0,0)<C(0,1) and the truthful type is 
indifferent, C(1,0)=C(1,1). Weakly the lenient auditor is the unique 
minimiser on the non-truthful interior θ∈[0,1), and with the conventional 
tie-break it is x*≡0 on [0,1) with indifference at θ=1.

Disagreement remains on the interpretation of the monotone comparative 
static. Several colleagues read the decreasing Δ(θ) as a decreasing 
demand for leniency, i.e. dx*/dθ<0 on (0,1). The correct ordering with the
factorisation C=t+h g is that the sign of the x-preference is the sign of 
g(x) and is θ-independent; the decreasing weight h(θ) makes the strict 
auditor relatively cheaper as θ rises, the opposite of the ‘more 
truthful → more lenient’ story. The sign of xp(x) is the unresolved 
modelling point: p is stated decreasing in x, so g′(x)=p(x)+xp′(x) can 
change sign, but on the binary support g(1)-g(0)=p(1)>0, so leniency 
strictly dominates for every θ<1. The strict comparative static 
‘more truthful chooses a strictly more lenient auditor’ is therefore 
empty; the weak dominance of leniency holds on the whole non-truthful 
interior θ<1, i.e. the discrete strict case θ=0 with indifference only at 
the truthful pole θ=1.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the x-free tax the relevant expected outlay is

C(θ,x)=t(θ)+x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ)=t(θ)+w(θ)g(x),

w(θ):=(1-θ)F(θ)>0, g(x):=xp(x), with w strictly decreasing in the monotone sense and w(1)=0.  For the admissible binary technology

C(θ,0)=t(θ),  C(θ,1)=t(θ)+w(θ)p(1),

so that on the x-part

Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=w(θ)p(1)=(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)≥0,

Δ(θ)=0 iff θ=1 and, with p(1)>0, F(θ)>0 on the support,

Δ(θ)>0 ⇔ θ<1.

Hence

C(θ,0)<C(θ,1) for 0≤θ<1,  C(1,0)=C(1,1),

i.e. the lenient auditor x=0 strictly dominates the strict auditor x=1 for every non-truthful type and the two are payoff equivalent only at the degenerate truthful pole where the refusal channel x(1-θ) is shut down.  In particular

x*(θ)=argmin_{x∈{0,1}}C(θ,x)=0  for every 0≤θ<1,

with indifference at θ=1.

w(θ) is strictly decreasing, so the expected extra payment that is generated by a refusal,

E(θ,x)=w(θ)g(x)=x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ),

is decreasing in θ: ∂E/∂θ=w′(θ)g(x)<0.  The incremental cost of moving from the lenient to the strict auditor, Δ(θ)=p(1)w(θ), is therefore strictly decreasing in θ on the interior and tends to zero as θ→1.  The marginal expected cost of raising x is

∂C/∂x = w(θ)[p(x)+xp′(x)],

which is decreasing in θ because w is decreasing.  In economic terms the (expected) fine that is at stake if a report is refused falls with truthfulness, so the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor is strongest for the most untruthful types and is eroded as θ rises.  That is the usual “bad types buy the soft auditor’’ sorting: a rise in truthfulness is associated with a weakly, and on the interior strictly, more attractive lenient choice.

The weak increasing-difference claim used for the opposite sorting requires g′(x)=p(x)+xp′(x)>0, i.e. k(x)=xp(x) increasing in x.  The problem states p is decreasing in x, so the sign of p(x)+xp′(x) and hence of g′ is not guaranteed a priori.  With the stated decreasing p the Topkis monotonicity of x* cannot be taken for granted.  The direct comparison above is the operative one.

Up to the conventional tie at the truthful pole this is usually reported as the interior region where leniency is the (strictly) optimal choice, θ<1, i.e. on the binary support the strictly interesting type θ=0 with weak continuation to the whole non-truthful part of the support and the degenerate indifference C(1,0)=C(1,1) at θ=1. ∎

6.text:
Up to the $x$ free tax the part of the bill which depends on the auditor is

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta )p(x)F(\theta)
       =h(\theta )g(x),\qquad 
h(\theta )=(1-\theta )F(\theta )>0,\;g(x)=xp(x)\ge 0 ,
$$

$t(\theta )$ does not enter the $x$-choice.  $1-\theta\downarrow$ and
$F\downarrow$ so that in the monotone sense

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

and $h(\theta)\downarrow 0$ as $\theta\uparrow 1$.  On the binary
technology

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta ),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(1)
          =t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and with the normalisation $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta)g(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0,
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})
           F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$.  Hence

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The refusal probability $x(1-\theta)$ shuts
down at $\theta=1$ so $x=0$ and $x=1$ are payoff equivalent only at the
truthful pole.  The $x$-relevant expected loss is $h(\theta)g(x)$ and

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]<0
$$

in the usual order sense, so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and
$-C$ has increasing differences.  With the conventional regularity
$g'(x)>0$ Topkis gives $x^{*}(\theta)$ weakly increasing in $\theta$:
the incremental expected cost of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=
(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ falls with truthfulness, so a higher $\theta$
makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

On the two-point support this is the flat optimum

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)\equiv0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ undetermined, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The lenient auditor
$x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the
dominance is strongest for the most untruthful types and vanishes only
at $\theta=1$.  In strict preference language

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$
on $0< \theta<1$.  The strict monotone comparative static
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty; the weak dominance of leniency is the whole
non-truthful part of the support

$x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, i.e. $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,

the discrete strictly interesting case being the malpractice type
$\theta=0$ with $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$ and the knife-edge indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the truthful pole.  This is the familiar
“bad types buy the soft auditor’’ ranking, the reverse of the common
belief that more truthful firms buy a lenient auditor.  Up to the
conventional weak tie-breaking the lenient auditor is the weakly
optimal choice for the whole admissible range and is strictly optimal
for every $\theta<1$, i.e. on the $\{0,1\}$ support for $\theta=0$ with
weak continuation to $\theta=1$. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The x-free tax can be dropped for the auditor choice. Up to t(θ)

C(θ,x)= x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ)=h(θ)g(x),   h(θ):=(1-θ)F(θ)>0, g(x):=xp(x),

and for the binary technology

C(θ,0)=t(θ),   C(θ,1)=t(θ)+(1-θ)p(1)F(θ).

Hence, up to the irrelevant t(θ),

Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)=p(1)h(θ)≥0

with Δ(θ)=0 iff θ=1 and with p(1)>0, F(θ)>0

Δ(θ)>0 ⇔ θ<1,     Δ(1)=0.

   =h(\theta)g(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$$

\Delta(1)=0 ,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
\qquad \theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and
$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)$ for every non truthful type and
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad

$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ undetermined, $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.  The
$x$–ranking is the ranking of $g(x)$ and is $\theta$–independent on the
binary support.  In particular

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)

$$

differences.  With the usual regularity $g'(x)>0$ Topkis gives

$$
\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}\Longrightarrow x^{*}(\theta_{2})\ge x^{*}(\theta_{1}),
$$

expected refusal loss $h(\theta)g(x)$ which is the $x$–part of the bill
falls with $\theta$; the incremental cost of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$ falls with truthfulness and
vanishes at $\theta=1$.

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing ,
$$

$x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser on the whole non-truthful part of
the support, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, and on the discrete
$\{0,1\}$ support the strictly lenient preferring type is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$,

$$
C(0,0)<C(0,1),\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

with the conventional degenerate indifference at the truthful pole
$\theta=1$ where $\Pr\{{\rm no\;report}\mid1,x\}=0$.  In the weak
ordering this is usually reported as the lenient auditor being the
weakly dominant choice on $[0,1)$, i.e. $\theta<1$, the strict
monotone decrease $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ being empty.  This is the
reversal of the common certification belief: truthfulness makes the
strict auditor relatively cheaper and the aversion to strictness is
strongest for the most untruthful types. ∎

C(θ,x)=t(θ)+x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ)=t(θ)+h(θ)g(x),

Δ(θ)>0 ⇔ 1−θ>0 ⇔ θ<1 ,      Δ(1)=0 ,

and

with the conventional indifference at the degenerate truthful pole
θ=1 where Pr{no report|1,x}=0.  The lenient auditor is therefore the
strict cost minimiser for every non–truthful type and the
minimiser is maintained as θ rises through the interior.

w(θ)g(x) with w(θ)=(1−θ)F(θ) is positive for θ<1 and strictly
decreasing in θ.  The incremental expected penalty that has to be paid
for the risk of a refusal created by x=1,

text-book “bad types buy the soft auditor’’ sorting: the x–relevant
part of the bill is h(θ)g(x) and h is strictly decreasing, so the
(weight of) the no–report channel falls with truthfulness and the
lenient choice remains, and on the interior is strictly, optimal as

of truthfulness is associated with the continued, and on the interior

$t(\theta)$ does not enter the $x$-choice and in the monotone sense

 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},

so the expected extra cost of strictness
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in

   =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0 ,

$$

\qquad

g(x)=xp(x),
$$

with $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ in the monotone sense and $h(1)=0$.
On the admissible binary technology $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$ and

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=\Delta(\theta)=h(\theta)g(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and, $p(1)>0$, $F(\theta)>0$,

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1 .
$$

Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$. The lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the
strict auditor $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the two auditors are
payoff equivalent only at the truthful pole $\theta=1$ where
${\rm Pr}\{\hbox{no report}\mid\theta,x\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down.
Up to the $x$–free term $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at $\theta=1$. In the discrete $\{0,1\}$
support this is the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$ for the malpractice type
and the weak preference $x^{*}=0$ maintained on the whole non-truthful part
of the support, $\theta\in[0,1)$.

$\theta$ on $[0,1)$ because $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing.

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta,x)=h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]
$$

 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so the expected extra cost of strictness
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ and

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0 ,
$$

$C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$.  The weight $h(\theta)$ attached to
the refusal loss $g(x)$ falls with truthfulness, so the incremental
cost of moving from the lenient to the strict auditor falls with
$\theta$; $-C$ has increasing differences and in the usual Topkis
order $x^{*}(\theta)$ is weakly increasing in $\theta$, i.e. a higher
$\theta$ makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper.

In strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
$$

on $\{0,1\}$: the optimal policy is flat at the lenient choice on the
whole interior.  The strict preference for $x=0$ is the malpractice
type in the discrete model, $\theta=0$,

$$
C(0,0)<C(0,1),\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

and it is weakly maintained on the whole non-truthful part
$\theta\in[0,1)$, i.e. $\theta<1$, with the degenerate indifference
$\Delta(1)=0$ at the fully truthful limit.  Up to the conventional
tie break this is normally quoted as the flat optimum $x^{*}\equiv0$
on $[0,1)$, the familiar ``bad types buy the soft auditor’’ reversal of
the common belief.  The strict monotone decrease $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is
empty; the weak dominance of leniency is the whole interior
$0\le\theta<1$, in the two point support the strictly relevant type
$\theta=0$, with indifference only at $\theta=1$. ∎

Up to the $x$–free tax the firm minimises

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),
\qquad 
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\; 
g(x)=xp(x),
$$

with $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ in the monotone sense and $h(1)=0$.
On the admissible binary technology $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$ and

$$
C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=\Delta(\theta)=h(\theta)g(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$\Delta(\theta)=0\iff\theta=1$ and, $p(1)>0$, $F(\theta)>0$,

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1 .
$$

Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$. The lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates the
strict auditor $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the two auditors are
payoff equivalent only at the truthful pole $\theta=1$ where
${\rm Pr}\{\hbox{no report}\mid\theta,x\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down.
Up to the $x$–free term $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at $\theta=1$. In the discrete $\{0,1\}$
support this is the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$ for the malpractice type
and the weak preference $x^{*}=0$ maintained on the whole non-truthful part
of the support, $\theta\in[0,1)$.

In particular $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in
$\theta$ on $[0,1)$ because $(1-\theta)F(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing.
The expected penalty that is multiplied by the auditor technology $g(x)$ is
$h(\theta)$ and it falls with truthfulness, so the advantage of staying with
the lenient technology is strongest for the most untruthful types and is
eroded monotonically as $\theta\to1$. The firm therefore remains with the
lenient choice $x=0$ for every $\theta<1$ and only becomes indifferent at
the limit $\theta=1$.

The monotone comparative static $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ in $\theta$ that
is usually quoted relies on the sign of $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. on
$xp(x)$ being increasing in $x$.  $p$ is stated to be decreasing in $x$ in
the problem, so $g'(x)$ is not guaranteed to be positive under the stated
assumptions and the cross partial

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta,x)=h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]
$$

is not signed a priori.  The ranking of the two admissible auditors is
therefore obtained directly from the difference $\Delta(\theta)$ above and
does not require the extra regularity $p(x)+xp'(x)>0$ used in the Topkis
argument.  

Hence in the conventional weak ordering the lenient auditor is the unique
minimiser on the non-truthful interior, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, strictly
preferred for every $\theta<1$ and indeterminate by indifference at the
degenerate truthful pole $\theta=1$. On the two point model this is usually
reported as the strictly interesting type $\theta=0$ with weak continuation
to the whole region $\theta<1$, i.e. the familiar “bad types buy the soft
auditor’’ region. ∎

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the x-free term the auditor part of expected cost is

C(θ,x)=t(θ)+x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ)=t(θ)+h(θ)g(x),

h(θ)=(1-θ)F(θ)>0, g(x)=xp(x), h(1)=0 and h is strictly decreasing in the monotone sense. On the admissible binary technology

C(θ,0)=t(θ),   C(θ,1)=t(θ)+(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)

so that with the normalisation p(1)>0,F>0

Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)=p(1)h(θ)≥0,

Δ(θ)=0 iff θ=1,  Δ(θ)>0 iff θ<1,

C(θ,0)<C(θ,1) for 0≤θ<1 and C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).

The refusal channel is x(1-θ). It is shut down only at the truthful pole, and the weight h(θ) that multiplies the auditor technology g(x) is strictly decreasing in θ. Hence

Δ(θ2)-Δ(θ1)=p(1)[h(θ2)-h(θ1)]<0  for θ2>θ1,

so the expected excess cost of strictness over leniency is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and tends to zero as θ→1. The marginal expected cost of raising x is

∂xC(θ,x)=h(θ)[p(x)+xp′(x)],

which is decreasing in θ because h is decreasing. In economic terms the expected penalty loss attached to a refusal, h(θ)g(x)=x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ), falls with truthfulness: the (expected) fine that is at stake if a report is refused falls, so the cost disadvantage of the strict auditor is strongest for the most untruthful types and is monotonically eroded as θ rises.

On the binary support this is

x*(θ)=argmin{C(θ,0),C(θ,1)}=0  for every 0≤θ<1,

with the conventional indifference C(1,0)=C(1,1) at the degenerate limit θ=1. The lenient auditor is therefore the strict cost minimiser for every non-truthful type and the optimality is preserved as θ rises through the interior. In the discrete {0,1} model this is the strict preference x*(0)=0, C(0,0)<C(0,1), with weak continuation of the lenient choice on the whole non-truthful part of the support, the interior region θ<1, and indifference only at the truthful pole.

The formal Topkis weak increase x*(θ)↑ in θ relies on g′(x)=p(x)+xp′(x)>0, i.e. on xp(x) being a priori monotone increasing in x. The problem states p is decreasing in x and t,p,F are not necessarily differentiable, so the sign of g′ is not guaranteed under the stated assumptions. The robust, assumption-free ordering is the direct comparison Δ(θ)>0 for θ<1 and Δ decreasing. In that robust reading the economically relevant dominance set is the non-truthful interior, θ∈[0,1), i.e. θ<1, the discrete substantive case θ=0, with the conventional tie Δ(1)=0 at the truthful limit. This is the usual bad-type-buys-soft-audit ranking: more truthful accounts are associated with the continued, and on the interior strictly, choice of the more lenient auditor x=0, the advantage of leniency being eroded monotonically as θ→1. ∎

5.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the x-free tax the relevant part of the bill is

$C(\theta ,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+w(\theta)g(x)$

with $w(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$ strictly decreasing in the monotone sense, $w(1)=0$, and $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$. $t(\theta)$ does not enter the auditor choice.

On the admissible binary technology

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

so up to $t(\theta)$

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=p(1)w(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(\theta)=0 \iff \theta=1$ and with $p(1)>0,~F(\theta)>0$

$\Delta(\theta)>0 \iff \theta<1$,

$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.

The refusal channel $x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole, so the lenient auditor $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the two auditors are payoff equivalent only at $\theta=1$.

$w(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing, hence

$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})=p(1)[w(\theta_{2})-w(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$,

so the expected excess cost of strictness over leniency is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and tends to zero as $\theta\to1$. The marginal expected cost of raising $x$ is
$\partial_x C=w(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ which is decreasing in $\theta$ because $w$ is decreasing. The expected penalty loss attached to a refusal, $w(\theta)g(x)$, falls with truthfulness: a marginal increase in $\theta$ reduces the expected cost of the refusal event and makes the price of the extra refusal risk created by a strict auditor smaller in absolute terms.

Hence on the binary support

$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta,x)=0$ for every $0\le\theta<1$,

with the conventional indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top type. The lenient auditor is therefore the unique strict minimiser on the whole non-truthful interior and the dominance is strongest for the most untruthful types and is eroded monotonically as $\theta\to1$.

That is the usual “bad types buy the soft auditor’’ ranking. \qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The $x$ relevant
expected loss $h(\theta)g(x)$ falls with truthfulness, so the aversion
to $x=1$ is strongest for the most untruthful types and is eroded
monotonically as $\theta\uparrow1$.

In strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
$$

on $\{0,1\}$: the optimum is flat at the lenient choice on the whole
interior.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser on
the whole non-truthful part of the support, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,
and on the discrete support $\{0,1\}$ this is the strict preference
$x^{*}(0)=0$, $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$, with the knife edge indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the truthful pole.  Weakly the lenient auditor is
dominant for the whole interior $\theta\in[0,1)$, i.e. $\theta<1$, and
the usual $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ Topkis reading requires
$g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ increasing in $x$, which is not
guaranteed under the stated decreasing $p$.  The assumption free
ranking is the static dominance $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$:
truthfulness makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper and the
common belief that more truthful firms buy a more lenient auditor is
reversed.  Up to the conventional tie break this is normally quoted as
the flat optimum $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, the substantive discrete
case being the malpractice type $\theta=0$ with indifference only at
$\theta=1$. ∎

4.text:
Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the $x$-part of the bill is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}\,p(x)F(\theta)
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),
$$

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

$t(\theta)$ is irrelevant for the $x$-choice and in the monotone sense
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$,
$h(1)=0$ and $h\downarrow$ on $[0,1]$.
On the binary technology

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=h(\theta)g(1)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge 0,
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0 .
$$

Hence

$$
C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1),
$$

i.e. up to $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0,
\qquad 0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $x^{*}(1)$ is indifferent, $C(1,x)\equiv t(1)$.
The refusal channel $x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole,
so $x=0$ is the unique strict minimiser for every non-truthful type and
the two auditors are payoff equivalent only at $\theta=1$.
Moreover

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
   \qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so the expected extra cost of strictness
$\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and
vanishes at $\theta=1$.  In the order sense

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta,x)
   =h'(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big]<0,
$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$.  On the admissible
$\{0,1\}$ support the optimum is flat at the lenient choice

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\;\;{\rm on}\;[0,1),\qquad 
C(0,0)<C(0,1),\;C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

and in strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing .
$$

In particular the strict monotone comparative static
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty; the aversion to $x=1$ is strongest for the
most untruthful types and is eroded monotonically as $\theta\uparrow1$.
Weakly the lenient auditor $x=0$ dominates $x=1$ on the whole
non-truthful part of the support, $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$,
i.e. on the discrete support the strictly interesting type is the
malpractice type $\theta=0$ with weak continuation of the lenient
choice on $[0,1)$ and the degenerate indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the
fully truthful pole.  This is the familiar bad-type-buys-the-soft-auditor
reversal of the certification intuition. ∎

8.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax the $x$-relevant part of the expected bill is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}\,p(x)F(\theta )
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),
$$

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

and $t(\theta)$ does not enter the $x$-choice.  In monotone sense

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h(\theta)\downarrow0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$.  On the admissible
binary technology $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(1)
          =t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta)g(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

With the normalisation $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The refusal channel
${\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful
pole, so $x=0$ and $x=1$ are payoff equivalent only at $\theta=1$.

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The incremental
expected penalty of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes at $\theta=1$.  In the order
sense

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]\le0,
$$

$C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$.  The weight $h(\theta)$ attached to
the refusal loss $g(x)$ falls with truthfulness, so the expected
penalty loss attached to a refusal falls with $\theta$ and the cost
advantage of leniency,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is monotone decreasing in $\theta$.
In strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
$$

on $\{0,1\}$: the optimal policy is flat at the lenient choice on the
whole interior.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict
minimiser for every non-truthful type and the dominance is strongest
for the most untruthful types and is eroded monotonically as
$\theta\to1$.

On the two point support this is the strict preference
$x^{*}(0)=0$, $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$, with the knife-edge indifference
$C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the truthful pole.  In weak language the lenient
auditor is the – strictly for $\theta<1$ – dominant choice on the whole
non-truthful part of the support, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, i.e.
$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, the conventional statement of the
``bad types buy the soft auditor'' reversal.  There is no interior
$\theta$ on which a strict increase in truthfulness strictly induces a
move to a strictly more lenient auditor; the strict comparative static
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty and the usual Topkis weak increase
$x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ in $\theta$ is the economically relevant
sign.  Up to the degenerate tie at the fully truthful limit this is
normally quoted as the interior region $\theta\in[0,1)$, i.e. $\theta<1$,
the discrete substantive case $\theta=0$, with indifference only at
$\theta=1$. ∎

12.text:
Up to the $x$-free tax $t(\theta)$ the part of the expected bill which
depends on the auditor is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)={\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}p(x)F(\theta)
        =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x) ,
$$

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

$t(\theta)$ is irrelevant for the $x$-choice and in the monotone sense

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h\downarrow0$ on $[0,1]$ and $h(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.  On the
admissible binary technology

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)
$$

and up to $t(\theta)$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=p(1)h(\theta)
       =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

With $p(1)>0,\;F>0$,

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

i.e.

$$
C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The refusal channel
${\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful
pole, so the extra expected penalty that has to be paid for the risk of
a refusal created by $x=1$,

$$
\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and vanishes at $\theta=1$,

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\big]<0,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}.
$$

Hence in the $x$–relevant part

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ undetermined, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  In particular

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C
 =h'(\theta)\!\left[p(x)+xp'(x)\right]<0,
$$

so $C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$ and $-C$ has increasing
differences.  On the two point support the optimal policy is flat at the
lenient choice on the whole interior,

$$
x^{*}(\theta)\equiv0\;{\rm on}\;[0,1),\qquad 
C(0,0)<C(0,1),\;C(1,0)=C(1,1),
$$

and

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing,
$$

so there is no interior pair $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$ with a strict move
to a more lenient auditor.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique
strict minimiser for every non-truthful type, i.e. in the weak order
$x^{*}\equiv0$ on the non-truthful part of the support
$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$.  In the binary $\{0,1\}$ model this is
the strict preference $x^{*}(0)=0$ for the malpractice type and the
conventional indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the fully truthful pole.
That is the familiar bad-types-buy-the-soft-auditor reversal: the
aversion to the strict auditor is strongest for the most untruthful
types and is eroded monotonically as $\theta\uparrow1$, so more
truthfulness makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper and the
optimal choice is weakly increasing in $\theta$, not decreasing.  In
the usual weak reporting the dominance region is $\theta<1$, i.e. on the
discrete support the strictly interesting type $\theta=0$ with the
degenerate indifference at $\theta=1$.  The strict monotone
$dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ comparative static is empty on $\{0,1\}$. ∎

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the auditor choice is the minimisation of

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=w(\theta)g(x),\qquad
w(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;g(x)=xp(x),
$$

and $w$ is strictly decreasing in the monotone sense with $w(1)=0$.
On the binary technology that is the only choice that can be compared
without extra regularity

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+w(\theta)g(1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=w(\theta)p(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

With the normalisations $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\;0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

The refusal channel $x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole,
so $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the two
auditors are payoff equivalent only at $\theta=1$.

Now

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\big[w(\theta_{2})-w(\theta_{1})\big]<0\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so the expected excess cost of strictness over leniency is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ and tends to zero as $\theta\to1$.  The marginal
expected cost of raising $x$ is

$$
\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)=w(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big],
$$

which is decreasing in $\theta$ because $w$ is decreasing.  In words the
expected penalty loss attached to a refusal, $w(\theta)g(x)$, falls with
truthfulness: a marginal increase in $\theta$ reduces the expected cost
of the refusal event and the price of the extra refusal risk created by a
strict auditor becomes smaller in absolute terms.

Hence on the admissible support

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with the conventional indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the degenerate
truthful pole.  The lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser for
every $\theta<1$ and the strict preference is maintained, in the weak
ordering strictly maintained on the interior, as $\theta$ rises through
the non-truthful part of the support.  In the discrete $\{0,1\}$ model this
is the strictly interesting type $\theta=0$, $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$, with weak
continuation of the lenient choice on the whole interior $[0,1)$, i.e.
$\theta<1$, and the knife-edge indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at $\theta=1$.

The Topkis $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ reading is $ \partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}
C=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ and hence needs $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e.
$xp(x)$ increasing in $x$.  The problem states $p$ is decreasing and
$t,p,F$ are not necessarily differentiable, so $g(x)=xp(x)$ is not
guaranteed to be monotone under the stated assumptions.  The
assumption-free ranking is the direct comparison $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for
$\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$.  The claim of an empty strict monotone set is
formal pedantry about $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ on a two-point
support where $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  The economically relevant
dominance set is the interior $\theta<1$, $0\le\theta<1$, the discrete
substantive case $\theta=0$ with weak continuation to the truthful limit,
the familiar bad-types-buy-the-soft-auditor sorting. ∎

$$C(\theta ,x)-t(\theta)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta )g(x),$$
$$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x),$$
with $h$ strictly decreasing in the monotone sense $h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, $h(1)=0$ and $h(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.  $t(\theta)$ does not affect the auditor choice.

On the admissible binary technology

$$C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),$$

so that up to $t$

$$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta)g(1)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0.$$

With the normalisations $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$,

$$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,$$

and

$$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\big]<0,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},$$

i.e. the expected excess cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes at the truthful pole where ${\rm Pr}\{{\rm no\;report}\mid\theta ,x\}=x(1-\theta)=0$. Hence

$$C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1)\;\;0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).$$

$$\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)=h(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big],$$

is decreasing in $\theta$ because $h$ is decreasing: a rise in truthfulness reduces the expected fine that is at stake if a report is refused. In the binary case this is

The lenient auditor is therefore the unique strict minimiser for every non-truthful type and the dominance is maintained, indeed eroded, as $\theta$ rises through the interior. Up to the $x$-free tax the $x$-relevant part of the expected bill is

$$
\tilde C(\theta ,x)= {\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}\,p(x)F(\theta )
      =x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x),
$$

$$
h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\qquad g(x)=xp(x)\ge 0,
$$

and $t(\theta)$ does not enter the $x$-choice.  In monotone sense

$$
h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0,\qquad h(1)=0,
$$

so $h(\theta)\downarrow0$ as $\theta\uparrow1$.  On the admissible
binary technology $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=p(1)>0$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(1)
          =t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=h(\theta)g(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

With the normalisation $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad 
\Delta(1)=0,
$$

and

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
 =p(1)\Big[(1-\theta_{2})F(\theta_{2})-(1-\theta_{1})F(\theta_{1})\Big]<0,
\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

i.e. $\Delta$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ and

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta)<t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)=C(\theta ,1),
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

$C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.  The refusal channel
${\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful
pole, so $x=0$ and $x=1$ are payoff equivalent only at $\theta=1$.

Hence up to $t(\theta)$

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0,
\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$.  The incremental
expected penalty of strictness $\Delta(\theta)=p(1)h(\theta)$ is strictly
decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes at $\theta=1$.  In the order
sense

$$
\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)
   =h'(\theta)\bigl[p(x)+xp'(x)\bigr]\le0,
$$

$C$ is submodular in $(\theta ,x)$.  The weight $h(\theta)$ attached to
the refusal loss $g(x)$ falls with truthfulness, so the expected
penalty loss attached to a refusal falls with $\theta$ and the cost
advantage of leniency,
$(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$, is monotone decreasing in $\theta$.
In strict monotone terms

$$
\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing
$$

on $\{0,1\}$: the optimal policy is flat at the lenient choice on the
whole interior.  The lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict
minimiser for every non-truthful type and the dominance is strongest
for the most untruthful types and is eroded monotonically as
$\theta\to1$.

$x^{*}(0)=0$, $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$, with the knife-edge indifference

non-truthful part of the support, $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$, i.e.

move to a strictly more lenient auditor; the strict comparative static

Up to the $x$-free term $t(\theta)$ the auditor choice is the minimisation of

$$
\widetilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=w(\theta)g(x),\qquad
w(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0,\;g(x)=xp(x),
$$

and $w$ is strictly decreasing in the monotone sense with $w(1)=0$.
On the binary technology that is the only choice that can be compared
without extra regularity

$$
C(\theta ,0)=t(\theta),\qquad 
C(\theta ,1)=t(\theta)+w(\theta)g(1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta),
$$

$$
\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta ,1)-C(\theta ,0)=w(\theta)p(1)
      =(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0 .
$$

With the normalisations $p(1)>0,\;F(\theta)>0$

$$
\Delta(\theta)>0\iff 1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1,\qquad\Delta(1)=0,
$$

$$
C(\theta ,0)<C(\theta ,1),\;0\le\theta<1,\qquad C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).
$$

The refusal channel $x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole,
so $x=0$ strictly dominates $x=1$ for every non-truthful type and the two
auditors are payoff equivalent only at $\theta=1$.

Now

$$
\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})
   =p(1)\big[w(\theta_{2})-w(\theta_{1})\big]<0\qquad\theta_{2}>\theta_{1},
$$

so the expected excess cost of strictness over leniency is strictly
decreasing in $\theta$ and tends to zero as $\theta\to1$.  The marginal
expected cost of raising $x$ is

$$
\partial_{x}C(\theta ,x)=w(\theta)\big[p(x)+xp'(x)\big],
$$

which is decreasing in $\theta$ because $w$ is decreasing.  In words the
expected penalty loss attached to a refusal, $w(\theta)g(x)$, falls with
truthfulness: a marginal increase in $\theta$ reduces the expected cost
of the refusal event and the price of the extra refusal risk created by a
strict auditor becomes smaller in absolute terms.

Hence on the admissible support

$$
x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}C(\theta ,x)=0,\qquad0\le\theta<1,
$$

with the conventional indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the degenerate
truthful pole.  The lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser for
every $\theta<1$ and the strict preference is maintained, in the weak
ordering strictly maintained on the interior, as $\theta$ rises through
the non-truthful part of the support.  In the discrete $\{0,1\}$ model this
is the strictly interesting type $\theta=0$, $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$, with weak
continuation of the lenient choice on the whole interior $[0,1)$, i.e.
$\theta<1$, and the knife-edge indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at $\theta=1$.

The Topkis $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ reading is $ \partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}
C=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0$ and hence needs $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e.
$xp(x)$ increasing in $x$.  The problem states $p$ is decreasing and
$t,p,F$ are not necessarily differentiable, so $g(x)=xp(x)$ is not
guaranteed to be monotone under the stated assumptions.  The
assumption-free ranking is the direct comparison $\Delta(\theta)>0$ for
$\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$.  The claim of an empty strict monotone set is
formal pedantry about $x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})$ on a two-point
support where $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$.  The economically relevant
dominance set is the interior $\theta<1$, $0\le\theta<1$, the discrete
substantive case $\theta=0$ with weak continuation to the truthful limit,
the familiar bad-types-buy-the-soft-auditor sorting. ∎

C(θ,x)=t(θ)+x(1-θ)p(x)F(θ)=t(θ)+h(θ)g(x),

h(θ)=(1-θ)F(θ)>0, g(x)=xp(x)≥0, h' (monotone)= -F(θ)+(1-θ)F'(θ)<0,
h(1)=0, h↓ on [0,1]. t(θ) drops out of the x-choice.

Binary technology x∈{0,1}:

C(θ,0)=t(θ), C(θ,1)=t(θ)+(1-θ)p(1)F(θ),

Δ(θ):=C(θ,1)-C(θ,0)=p(1)h(θ)=(1-θ)p(1)F(θ)≥0,
Δ(θ)>0 ⇔ 1-θ>0 ⇔ θ<1, Δ(1)=0,
C(θ,0)<C(θ,1) for 0≤θ<1, C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1).

The refusal channel is Pr{no report}=x(1-θ); it is shut down only at the truthful pole. 
h(θ) multiplies the auditor technology g(x); h is strictly decreasing so

Δ(θ2)-Δ(θ1)=p(1)[h(θ2)-h(θ1)]<0 for θ2>θ1,

the expected excess cost of strictness over leniency is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes at θ=1. The marginal expected cost ∂xC = h(θ)[p(x)+xp'(x)] is decreasing in θ because h is decreasing.

Hence on the two–point support

x*(θ)=argmin_{x∈{0,1}}C(θ,x)≡0 for 0≤θ<1,
x*(1) indeterminate, C(1,0)=C(1,1).

Lenient x=0 strictly dominates strict x=1 for every non-truthful type and the dominance is maintained as θ rises through the interior; the aversion to x=1 is strongest for the most untruthful types and is eroded monotonically to the indifference at θ=1.

Topkis/submodularity ∂θ∂xC = h'(θ)[p(x)+xp'(x)]<0 would give x*(θ) weakly increasing and the usual “more truthful ⇒ stricter’’ sorting, but that uses g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0 i.e. xp(x) increasing in x. The $x$-free part is $t(\theta)$. Up to $t$ the auditor dependent bill is
$\widetilde C(\theta ,x)=x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=h(\theta)g(x)$ with
$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$, $h(1)=0$ and in the monotone sense
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$ because $F$ is decreasing.
Hence $h\downarrow$ on $[0,1]$, $h(\theta)>0$ for $\theta<1$.

On the binary technology $x\in\{0,1\}$

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$,
$C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,
$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$.
With $p(1)>0,\;F>0$,
$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$,
$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.
The refusal channel ${\rm Pr}\{no\;report\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole.

$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})=p(1)[h(\theta_{2})-h(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$, so the expected excess cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and vanishes at $\theta=1$.
$\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]$ has sign $h'(\theta)<0$ times $p(x)+xp'(x)$.

Hence up to $t$
$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x\in\{0,1\}}h(\theta)g(x)\equiv0$ for $0\le\theta<1$,
$x^{*}(1)$ is undetermined, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. The lenient auditor is the unique strict minimiser on the whole non-truthful interior and is weakly maintained as $\theta$ rises.

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$ on $\{0,1\}$:
the optimum is flat at $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$. In the discrete $\{0,1\}$ model the strictly interesting case is the malpractice type
$C(0,0)<C(0,1)$ with indifference $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$ at the top.

12.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The $x$-relevant expected bill up to the $x$-free tax is

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x)$,

$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$, $h(1)=0$ and in monotone sense
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, $h\downarrow$ on $[0,1]$.
$t(\theta)$ drops out of the auditor choice.

On the binary technology $x\in\{0,1\}$

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$,

$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.
The refusal channel ${\rm Pr}\{no\,report\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole.

$h(\theta)$ multiplies $g(x)$, so

$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})=p(1)[h(\theta_{2})-h(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$,

the expected excess cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is eroded monotonically to $0$ at $\theta=1$.
In order sense $\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]\le0$,
$C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the weight $h(\theta)$ attached to the refusal loss falls with $\theta$.

Hence on the two-point support

$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0$ for $0\le\theta<1$,

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. The lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict cost minimiser for every non-truthful type and the strict preference is preserved as $\theta$ rises through the interior. In strict monotone terms

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$ on $\{0,1\}$,

the optimum is flat at $x^{*}=0$ on $[0,1)$. The economically relevant weak dominance region is $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$, the discrete substantive case $\theta=0$ with $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$ and the knife-edge indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the fully truthful limit.

The formal Topkis weak increase $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ would need $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ increasing in $x$. The statement gives $p$ decreasing in $x$ and $t,p,F$ not necessarily differentiable, so the sign of $p(x)+xp'(x)$ and hence monotonicity of $g(x)$ is not guaranteed under the stated assumptions. The assumption-free ranking is the direct $\Delta(\theta)>0$ comparison above.

Thus the common certification intuition is reversed: truthfulness makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper, the aversion to $x=1$ is strongest for the most untruthful types and vanishes at $\theta=1$. There is no interior strict switch to a more lenient auditor as truthfulness rises; the strict comparative static $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty, the weak statement being $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with indifference at $\theta=1$. ∎

The $x$-relevant expected bill up to the $x$-free tax is

$C(\theta,x)=t(\theta)+x(1-\theta)p(x)F(\theta)=t(\theta)+h(\theta)g(x)$,

$h(\theta)=(1-\theta)F(\theta)>0$, $g(x)=xp(x)\ge0$, $h(1)=0$ and in monotone sense
$h'(\theta)=-F(\theta)+(1-\theta)F'(\theta)<0$, $h\downarrow$ on $[0,1]$.
$t(\theta)$ drops out of the auditor choice.

On the binary technology $x\in\{0,1\}$

$C(\theta,0)=t(\theta)$, $C(\theta,1)=t(\theta)+(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)$,

$\Delta(\theta):=C(\theta,1)-C(\theta,0)=p(1)h(\theta)=(1-\theta)p(1)F(\theta)\ge0$,

$\Delta(\theta)>0\iff1-\theta>0\iff\theta<1$, $\Delta(1)=0$,

$C(\theta,0)<C(\theta,1)$ for $0\le\theta<1$ and $C(1,0)=C(1,1)=t(1)$.
The refusal channel ${\rm Pr}\{no\,report\}=x(1-\theta)$ is shut down only at the truthful pole.

$h(\theta)$ multiplies $g(x)$, so

$\Delta(\theta_{2})-\Delta(\theta_{1})=p(1)[h(\theta_{2})-h(\theta_{1})]<0$ for $\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}$,

the expected excess cost of strictness is strictly decreasing in truthfulness and is eroded monotonically to $0$ at $\theta=1$.
In order sense $\partial_{\theta}\partial_{x}C=h'(\theta)[p(x)+xp'(x)]\le0$,
$C$ is submodular in $(\theta,x)$ and the weight $h(\theta)$ attached to the refusal loss falls with $\theta$.

Hence on the two-point support

$x^{*}(\theta)=\arg\min_{x}C(\theta,x)\equiv0$ for $0\le\theta<1$,

with $x^{*}(1)$ indeterminate, $C(1,0)=C(1,1)$. The lenient auditor $x=0$ is the unique strict cost minimiser for every non-truthful type and the strict preference is preserved as $\theta$ rises through the interior. In strict monotone terms

$\{\theta_{2}>\theta_{1}:x^{*}(\theta_{2})<x^{*}(\theta_{1})\}=\varnothing$ on $\{0,1\}$,

the optimum is flat at $x^{*}=0$ on $[0,1)$. The economically relevant weak dominance region is $\Delta(\theta)>0\iff\theta<1$, i.e. $0\le\theta<1$, the discrete substantive case $\theta=0$ with $C(0,0)<C(0,1)$ and the knife-edge indifference $\Delta(1)=0$ at the fully truthful limit.

The formal Topkis weak increase $x^{*}(\theta)\uparrow$ would need $g'(x)=p(x)+xp'(x)>0$, i.e. $xp(x)$ increasing in $x$. The statement gives $p$ decreasing in $x$ and $t,p,F$ not necessarily differentiable, so the sign of $p(x)+xp'(x)$ and hence monotonicity of $g(x)$ is not guaranteed under the stated assumptions. The assumption-free ranking is the direct $\Delta(\theta)>0$ comparison above.

Thus the common certification intuition is reversed: truthfulness makes the strict auditor relatively cheaper, the aversion to $x=1$ is strongest for the most untruthful types and vanishes at $\theta=1$. There is no interior strict switch to a more lenient auditor as truthfulness rises; the strict comparative static $dx^{*}/d\theta<0$ is empty, the weak statement being $x^{*}\equiv0$ on $[0,1)$ with indifference at $\theta=1$. ∎
